### Problem: Presents {#sec-idx-p5-presents}

::: {.p-statement}
Petya invited $n$ friends ($1 \le n \le 100$), numbered $1..n$. Friend $i$ gave a present to friend $p_i$, and every friend received exactly one present, so $p$ is a permutation (a friend may give to themselves). Given $p$, print for each friend $j = 1..n$ the number of the friend who gave a present to $j$. Samples: $[2, 3, 4, 1] \to [4, 1, 2, 3]$; $[1, 3, 2] \to [1, 3, 2]$; $[1, 2] \to [1, 2]$.

Source: [CF 136A · Presents](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/136/A){.solved rating="800"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Read $p$ as the function "giver $\mapsto$ receiver". The question asks for its inverse, "receiver $\mapsto$ giver". One pass builds it: friend $i$ gave to $p_i$, so write $i$ into slot $p_i$ of the answer, $q_{p_i} = i$. The array indexes itself; no search and no map.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Search for each receiver.** For every $j$, scan $p$ for the $i$ with $p_i = j$. $O(n^2)$: the literal definition.
2. **Inverse by scatter.** For every $i$, set $q[p_i] = i$. Each write is $O(1)$, so the whole inverse costs $O(n)$. *Scatter* means writing to the position named by the data, the opposite of *gather*, which reads from it ($r_i = p[q_i]$).

**Invariant.** After processing givers $1..i$, $q_j$ is correct for every receiver $j$ that one of them gave to, and the other entries are still unset. Because $p$ is a bijection, every slot is written exactly once, and $q = p^{-1}$: $q_{p_i} = i$ and $p_{q_j} = j$.

**Worked trace.** $p = [2, 3, 4, 1]$: friend $1$ gave to $2$, so $q_2 = 1$; friend $2$ gave to $3$, so $q_3 = 2$; friend $3$ gave to $4$, so $q_4 = 3$; friend $4$ gave to $1$, so $q_1 = 4$. Output $[4, 1, 2, 3]$.
:::

::: {#fig-idx-p5-presents}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    perm = [2, 3, 4, 1]
    q = [0] * 4
    for i, v in enumerate(perm, 1):
        q[v - 1] = i
    assert q == [4, 1, 2, 3]
    V.array(ax, p, perm, label="p: giver -> receiver")
    V.array(ax, p, q, y=-3.4, label="q: receiver -> giver", colors={j: "green" for j in range(4)})
    for i, v in enumerate(perm):
        V.arrow(ax, p, i + 0.5, -0.1, v - 1 + 0.5, -2.3, color="indigo")
V.show(draw)
```

The first sample. Each arrow starts at giver $i$ in the top row and ends at slot $p_i$ of the bottom row, where it writes $i$. The bottom row is the inverse permutation $q = [4, 1, 2, 3]$ (cells are 0-based, values 1-based).

:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Search for each receiver

::: {.form-next}
For every receiver $j$, scan the givers for the one with $p_i = j$. Two nested loops, $O(n^2)$; fine at $n \le 100$ and exactly what the statement says.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("presents", "brute")
    assert str(final) == "[4, 1, 2, 3]"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def presents_brute(p):
    n = len(p)
    q = [0] * n
    for j in range(1, n + 1):
        for i in range(n):
            if p[i] == j:
                q[j - 1] = i + 1
                break
    return q


assert presents_brute([2, 3, 4, 1]) == [4, 1, 2, 3]       # the board sample
assert presents_brute([1, 3, 2]) == [1, 3, 2]
```

##### C++

```cpp
vector<int> presentsBrute(const vector<int>& p) {
    int n = (int)p.size();
    vector<int> q(n);
    for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++)
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
            if (p[i] == j) { q[j - 1] = i + 1; break; }
    return q;
}
```

:::

#### Inverse by scatter

::: {.form-next}
Turn each arrow around in one pass: giver $i$ writes $i$ into slot $p_i$. $O(n)$ time; this is the inverse permutation, the building block for composing and undoing permutations (@sec-idx-a6).
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("presents", "inverse")
    assert str(final) == "[4, 1, 2, 3]"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def presents(p):
    n = len(p)
    q = [0] * n
    for i in range(n):
        q[p[i] - 1] = i + 1
    return q


assert presents([2, 3, 4, 1]) == [4, 1, 2, 3]             # the board sample
assert presents([1, 3, 2]) == [1, 3, 2]
assert presents([1, 2]) == [1, 2]
for _ in range(300):
    n = random.randint(1, 12)
    p = random.sample(range(1, n + 1), n)
    q = presents(p)
    assert q == presents_brute(p)
    assert all(p[q[j] - 1] == j + 1 for j in range(n))    # p after q is the identity
    assert presents(q) == p                               # the inverse of the inverse
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    int n;
    scanf("%d", &n);
    vector<int> q(n + 1);
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
        int to;
        scanf("%d", &to);
        q[to] = i;                        // the present at `to` came from i
    }
    for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++) printf("%d ", q[j]);
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
```

:::

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Search for each receiver:** $O(n^2)$ time, $O(n)$ space for the output. **Inverse by scatter:** $O(n)$ time, $O(n)$ space for the output.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- The identity (everyone gives to themselves): $q = p$.
- An involution (every cycle of length $1$ or $2$, like $[1, 3, 2]$): again $q = p$. In general $q = p$ exactly when $p$ has no cycle longer than $2$.
- A single $n$-cycle $[2, 3, \ldots, n, 1]$: $q = [n, 1, 2, \ldots, n - 1]$, the rotation the other way.
- The scatter needs a bijection: if two givers shared a receiver, the later write would overwrite the earlier.
- `q[i] = p[p[i]]` is a gather; it computes $p \circ p$, not $p^{-1}$.
:::
